docs.title: Welcome to ArduVault!
docs.text: Welcome to Arduino Projects, a collection of tutorials and examples to help you learn and experiment with Arduino! Whether you are a beginner or an advanced maker, this site has something for you.

docs.title: What You Will Find Here
docs.text:
• Step-by-step tutorials for Arduino projects.
  • Example code that is easy to copy and use.
  • Clear explanations of components and concepts.
  • Tips for building, testing, and expanding your projects.

docs.title: How to Use This Site
docs.text:
1. Browse the Projects section to find topics of interest.
  2. Click on a project to see detailed instructions and example code.
  3. Copy the code into your Arduino IDE and experiment.
  4. Learn from the explanations and modify the projects to create your own versions.

docs.title: Featured Projects
docs.text:
• LED Blink – Learn to control LEDs.
  • Servo Motor Control – Learn to control a servo motor.

  • L298N – Learn how to use a L298N DC motor.
  • Ultrasonic Sensor – Learn how to use a Ultrasonic sensor.
  • Temperature Sensor – Learn how to use the Temperature sensor.

docs.title: Arduino Infrared Sensor with LED Indicator
docs.text: This project demonstrates how to use an infrared (IR) sensor with an LED to detect the presence of an object. When the sensor detects something in front of it, the LED automatically turns on and blinks.

docs.title: 1. Basic Concept
docs.text:
An infrared sensor emits infrared light and detects the reflection from nearby objects. When an object is detected, the sensor’s digital output changes — this signal can then be used to trigger other components, such as an LED.

With Arduino, we can easily read the sensor’s digital output and control an LED or any other actuator in response.

docs.title: 2. Working Principle
docs.text:
The IR sensor outputs a HIGH (1) or LOW (0) signal based on whether it detects an object.

HIGH (1): Object detected

LOW (0): No object detected

The Arduino reads this signal using digitalRead().

When detection occurs, the Arduino turns the LED ON for 0.5 seconds, then turns it OFF.

The Serial Monitor shows the live sensor readings in real time.

docs.title: 3. Main Components
docs.text: Component Function Arduino Board Processes the sensor input and controls the LED output. Infrared Sensor Detects objects using infrared reflection. LED Lights up when an object is detected. Resistor Limits current to protect the LED (typically 220Ω–330Ω). Jumper Wires Connects components to the Arduino pins. Breadboard Makes circuit assembly simple and clean.

docs.title: 4. Circuit Connection
docs.text: Component Arduino Pin Description Infrared Sensor OUT D6 Sensor digital output signal LED (Anode) D5 LED control pin LED (Cathode) GND Ground connection Sensor VCC 5V Power supply Sensor GND GND Common ground

docs.title: Example Code: Led Plus Infrared Example
docs.text:
int infrared = 6;   // Infrared sensor connected to digital pin 6
int LED = 5;        // LED connected to digital pin 5

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED, OUTPUT);     // Set the LED pin as output
  pinMode(infrared, INPUT); // Set the infrared sensor pin as input
  Serial.begin(9600);       // Start Serial Monitor to display data
}

void loop() {
  int sensorValue = digitalRead(infrared); // Read the digital value from the sensor (0 or 1)
  Serial.println(sensorValue);             // Print the value to the Serial Monitor

  if (sensorValue == 1) {                  
    digitalWrite(LED, HIGH);      // Turn the LED on
    delay(500);                   // Keep the LED on for 0.5 seconds
    digitalWrite(LED, LOW);       // Turn the LED off
    delay(500);                   
  } 
  else {                         
    digitalWrite(LED, LOW);       // Keep the LED off when no object is detected
    delay(100);                  
  }
}

docs.title: Arduino Dual Motor Control with L298N Driver
docs.text: This project demonstrates how to control two DC motors using an L298N motor driver and an Arduino. With this setup, you can make your motors move forward, backward, and stop, as well as control their speed using PWM (Pulse Width Modulation).

docs.title: 1. Basic Concept
docs.text: The L298N Motor Driver is an integrated circuit that allows Arduino to control the direction and speed of DC motors. Since Arduino pins cannot supply enough current to drive motors directly, the L298N acts as an interface — it amplifies control signals from the Arduino and provides sufficient current and voltage to the motors.

docs.title: 2. Working Principle
docs.text:
The L298N has two H-Bridge circuits, which allow independent control of two motors (A and B).

Each motor has:

Two direction control pins (IN1, IN2 for Motor A and IN3, IN4 for Motor B).

One enable pin (ENA for Motor A and ENB for Motor B) that controls speed using PWM (analogWrite).

By sending HIGH or LOW signals to the direction pins, you can make the motor rotate:

Forward

Backward

Stop

The speed is controlled by changing the PWM value (0–255) on the enable pins.

Component Function Arduino Board Sends control signals (PWM and logic) to the L298N driver. L298N Motor Driver Controls the speed and direction of two DC motors. DC Motors (x2) Convert electrical energy into motion. External Power Supply (e.g., 9V–12V) Provides sufficient current for the motors. Jumper Wires Connects Arduino to the L298N module. Breadboard (optional) Helps with clean and easy wiring.

docs.title: 4. Circuit Connection
docs.text: L298N Pin Arduino Pin Description ENA D3 PWM pin for Motor A speed control IN1 D8 Direction control 1 for Motor A IN2 D7 Direction control 2 for Motor A ENB D4 PWM pin for Motor B speed control IN3 D6 Direction control 1 for Motor B IN4 D5 Direction control 2 for Motor B +12V External Power (+) Power supply for motors (9–12V recommended) GND Arduino GND Common ground connection 5V (optional) Arduino 5V Power for logic (if jumper is installed on the L298N board)

docs.title: Example Code: Basic Motor Movement
docs.text:
// Motor A: left motor
// Motor B: right motor

#define ENA 3  // PWM pin for motor A speed control
#define IN1 8  // Direction pin 1 for motor A
#define IN2 7  // Direction pin 2 for motor A
#define ENB 4  // PWM pin for motor B speed control
#define IN3 6  // Direction pin 1 for motor B
#define IN4 5  // Direction pin 2 for motor B

void setup() {
  pinMode(ENA, OUTPUT); // Set ENA as output (speed control)
  pinMode(IN1, OUTPUT); // Set IN1 as output (motor A direction)
  pinMode(IN2, OUTPUT); // Set IN2 as output (motor A direction)
  pinMode(ENB, OUTPUT); // Set ENB as output (speed control)
  pinMode(IN3, OUTPUT); // Set IN3 as output (motor B direction)
  pinMode(IN4, OUTPUT); // Set IN4 as output (motor B direction)
}

void loop() {
  forward(200);   // Move both motors forward at speed 200
  delay(2000);    // Wait 2 seconds

  backward(200);  // Move both motors backward at speed 200
  delay(2000);    // Wait 2 seconds

  stopMotors();   // Stop both motors
  delay(2000);    // Wait 2 seconds
}

void forward(int speed) {
  digitalWrite(IN1, HIGH); // Motor A forward
  digitalWrite(IN2, LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN3, HIGH); // Motor B forward
  digitalWrite(IN4, LOW);
  analogWrite(ENA, speed); // Set motor A speed
  analogWrite(ENB, speed); // Set motor B speed
}

void backward(int speed) {
  digitalWrite(IN1, LOW);  // Motor A backward
  digitalWrite(IN2, HIGH);
  digitalWrite(IN3, LOW);  // Motor B backward
  digitalWrite(IN4, HIGH);
  analogWrite(ENA, speed); // Set motor A speed
  analogWrite(ENB, speed); // Set motor B speed
}

void stopMotors() {
  digitalWrite(IN1, LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN2, LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN3, LOW);
  digitalWrite(IN4, LOW);
  analogWrite(ENA, 0); // Stop motor A
  analogWrite(ENB, 0); // Stop motor B
}

docs.title: Arduino LED Control
docs.text: This project demonstrates how to control an LED using Arduino. You can turn the LED on and off, make it blink, and even control its brightness with PWM (Pulse Width Modulation).

docs.title: 1. Basic Concept
docs.text: An LED (Light Emitting Diode) emits light when current flows through it. Using Arduino, you can control the LED digitally (on/off) or analogically (brightness) with precise timing.

docs.title: 2. Working Principle
docs.text:
1. The Arduino sends a HIGH or LOW signal to the LED pin.
  2. HIGH turns the LED on.
  3. LOW turns the LED off.
  4. Using PWM (analogWrite), the Arduino can adjust the duty cycle to control the LED’s brightness.
  5. A current-limiting resistor protects the LED from burning out.

docs.title: 3. Main Components
docs.text: Component Function Arduino Board Provides control signals and power. LED Converts electrical energy into light. Resistor Limits current to prevent LED damage. Jumper Wires Connect components to Arduino pins. Breadboard Holds components for easy wiring.

docs.title: 4. Circuit Connection
docs.text: Component Arduino Pin Description LED Anode (+) D5 Connect to Arduino digital pin for control. LED Cathode (–) GND (through resistor) Connect to ground via a 220Ω–330Ω resistor.

docs.title: Example Code: Basic Blink
docs.text:
int ledPin = 13; // Pin connected to the LED

void setup() {
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT); // Set the LED pin as output
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH); // Turn the LED on
  delay(1000);                 // Wait 1 second

  digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);  // Turn the LED off
  delay(1000);                 // Wait 1 second
}

docs.title: Servo Motor
docs.text: A servo motor is a type of motor designed for precise control of angular or linear position, velocity, and acceleration. It operates as part of a closed-loop control system that constantly monitors and adjusts its motion to achieve accurate positioning.

docs.title: 1. Basic Concept
docs.text: A servo motor system consists of: A motor (DC or AC) A feedback device (encoder or potentiometer) A control circuit (servo controller or driver) The feedback device continuously measures the motor’s position, and the control circuit adjusts the motor’s movement to match the desired value.

docs.title: 2. Working Principle
docs.text: An input signal specifies the desired position. The controller compares this input with the feedback signal from the sensor. The error signal (difference between desired and actual position) is generated. The controller drives the motor to correct the error. The motor stops when the error reaches zero. This process is called closed-loop control, as it constantly checks and corrects the position.

docs.title: 3. Main Components
docs.text: Component Function Motor Provides the mechanical motion. Gearbox Reduces speed and increases torque. Feedback Sensor Measures shaft position and provides feedback. Control Circuit Compares input and feedback signals and drives the motor accordingly.

docs.title: 4. Circuit Connection
docs.text: Servo Pin (Wire Color) Arduino Pin Description Signal (Orange/Yellow) D9 Receives PWM signal from Arduino to control the angle. VCC (Red) 5V Powers the servo motor. GND (Brown/Black) GND Common ground connection with Arduino.

docs.title: Example Code: Basic Turn Principles
docs.text:
#include <Servo.h>  // Include Servo library

Servo myServo;      // Create Servo object

void setup() {
  myServo.attach(9);  // Attach servo signal to pin 9
}

void loop() {
  myServo.write(0);    // Move to 0 degrees
  delay(1000);         // Wait 1 second

  myServo.write(90);   // Move to 90 degrees
  delay(1000);         // Wait 1 second

  myServo.write(180);  // Move to 180 degrees
  delay(1000);         // Wait 1 second

  myServo.write(90);   // Return to 90 degrees
  delay(1000);         // Wait 1 second
}

docs.title: Arduino Temperature Sensor with Serial Monitor Display
docs.text: This project demonstrates how to use an LM35 temperature sensor with Arduino to measure and display the temperature in Celsius on the Serial Monitor in real time.

docs.title: 1. Basic Concept
docs.text:
The LM35 is an analog temperature sensor that outputs a voltage proportional to the surrounding temperature. By reading this analog voltage using Arduino’s analog input pin, we can easily calculate the temperature in degrees Celsius.

The result is continuously displayed in the Serial Monitor, updating every second.

docs.title: 2. Working Principle
docs.text:
The LM35 outputs an analog voltage that increases by 10 mV for every 1°C of temperature.

Arduino reads this voltage as a value between 0 and 1023 (from its 10-bit ADC). We then convert this value into Celsius using a simple formula:

Temperature (°C) = Analog Value × 5.0 × 100.0 1024.0 Temperature (°C)= 1024.0 Analog Value×5.0×100.0 ​

The Serial Monitor displays the temperature readings in real time.

docs.title: 3.Main Components
docs.text: Component Function Arduino Board Reads analog input and processes temperature data. LM35 Sensor Measures temperature and outputs proportional analog voltage. Jumper Wires Connects sensor pins to the Arduino board. Breadboard Simplifies circuit connections. USB Cable Powers Arduino and enables Serial Monitor communication.

docs.title: 4.Circuit Connection
Arduino Ultrasonic Distance Measurement
docs.text: This project demonstrates how to use an Ultrasonic Sensor (HC-SR04) with Arduino to measure the distance of an object. The sensor sends out an ultrasonic pulse and measures how long it takes for the echo to return — allowing you to calculate how far away an object is.

docs.title: 1. Basic Concept
docs.text: An ultrasonic sensor measures distance using sound waves. It emits a short ultrasonic pulse from the TRIG pin and waits for the reflection (echo) to return to the ECHO pin. By calculating the time difference, the Arduino can determine the distance between the sensor and the object.

docs.title: 2. Working Principle
docs.text:
The TRIG pin sends a short 10-microsecond pulse to start the measurement.

The ECHO pin receives the reflected sound wave (echo) from the object.

The Arduino measures how long the echo pin stays HIGH (time of flight).

Using the speed of sound (≈ 0.034 cm/µs),

Arduino calculates the distance:

Distance (cm) = Duration × 0.034 2 Distance (cm)= 2 Duration×0.034 ​

The division by 2 accounts for the signal traveling to the object and back.

docs.title: 3. Main Components
docs.text: Component Function Arduino Board Sends and receives signals to calculate distance. Ultrasonic Sensor (HC-SR04) Measures distance by using sound wave reflection. Jumper Wires Connect the sensor to the Arduino pins. Breadboard Simplifies wiring connections. USB Cable Powers the Arduino and allows serial data viewing on your computer.

docs.title: 4. Circuit Connection
docs.text: Ultrasonic Sensor Pin Arduino Pin Description VCC 5V Powers the ultrasonic sensor. GND GND Common ground with Arduino. TRIG D9 Sends the trigger pulse to start measurement. ECHO D10 Receives the reflected echo signal.

docs.title: Example Code: Basic Ultrasonic Distance Reading
docs.text:
#define TRIG_PIN 9   // The TRIG pin of the sensor is connected to Arduino pin 9
#define ECHO_PIN 10  // The ECHO pin of the sensor is connected to Arduino pin 10

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);        // Start serial communication at 9600 bps to view data in Serial Monitor
  pinMode(TRIG_PIN, OUTPUT); // Set TRIG pin as output (to send the signal)
  pinMode(ECHO_PIN, INPUT);  // Set ECHO pin as input (to receive the reflected signal)
}

void loop() {
  long duration;  // Variable to store the time the echo signal lasts
  float distance; // Variable to store the calculated distance in centimeters

  // Send a 10 microsecond pulse from TRIG to start the measurement
  digitalWrite(TRIG_PIN, LOW);      // Ensure TRIG is initially LOW (0V)
  delayMicroseconds(2);             // Wait for 2 microseconds
  digitalWrite(TRIG_PIN, HIGH);     // Set TRIG HIGH (5V)
  delayMicroseconds(10);            // Keep it HIGH for 10 microseconds
  digitalWrite(TRIG_PIN, LOW);      // Set TRIG back to LOW (0V)

  // Measure how long the ECHO pin stays HIGH (the time it takes for the sound to return)
  duration = pulseIn(ECHO_PIN, HIGH);

  // Calculate the distance in centimeters
  // Speed of sound ≈ 0.034 cm per microsecond
  // Divide by 2 because the signal travels to the object and back
  distance = duration * 0.034 / 2;

  // Display the distance in the Serial Monitor
  Serial.print("Distance: ");
  Serial.print(distance);
  Serial.println(" cm");

  delay(500); // Wait half a second before the next measurement
}
